OpenStax Biology 2e, 45.6 Community Ecology (symbiosis and parasitism)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 24.3 Ecology of Fungi (mutualism and commensalism)
NOAA Fagatele Bay National Marine Sanctuary, Clownfish and Sea Anemone
National Geographic, Beautiful Friendship (clownfish and anemones)

note.text: A sea anemone is an animal related to jellyfish. It clings to the reef and stays in one place.
Its tentacles are covered in stinging cells that catch prey and drive off predators.
A slimy mucus coat keeps the anemone from stinging the clownfish, so it can hide among the tentacles.
The anemone's stings protect the clownfish and its eggs from fish that would eat them.

steps.title: Defense
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow of the clownfish chasing it.

note.text: The clownfish chases off anemone-eating fish. It also cleans algae off its anemone.
This partnership is found on coral reefs in warm, shallow seas.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the clownfish orange, leaving the stripes white.

steps.title: Kind of symbiosis
steps.question: Both the clownfish and the anemone benefit. What kind of symbiosis is this?

options.feedback: Yes. In mutualism, both partners benefit.
In commensalism one partner benefits and the other isn't affected. Here both benefit.
A parasite harms its host. Neither partner is harmed here.
Neither one eats the other. They help each other.

steps.title: Parasitism
steps.question: A tick feeds on a deer's blood, weakening the deer. What kind of relationship is that?

options.text: Parasitism: the tick benefits and the deer is harmed
options.feedback: Right. A parasite lives on or in a host and takes nutrients from it.
The deer doesn't benefit. It's harmed, so this is parasitism.
In commensalism the other partner isn't affected. The deer is harmed.
They aren't competing for a resource. The tick feeds on the deer: parasitism.

steps.title: Predict
steps.question: Divers remove all the clownfish from a reef. What would you predict for the anemones?

options.text: More of them get eaten by butterflyfish
options.feedback: Yes. Without clownfish chasing them off, anemone-eating fish can feed more easily.
The clownfish defended the anemones. Losing them leaves the anemones less protected.
Anemones mostly stay put. They'd be less protected from predators.
Anemones can't do that. Without defenders, more would be eaten.
